content.title: salary
content.body:
Etymology

From salarie , from salarie , from salaire , from salārium , the neuter form of the adjective salārius , from salt . There have been various attempts to explain how the Latin term for “wages” came from the adjective “related to salt”. It is generally assumed that salārium was an abbreviation of salārium argentum , though that phrase is not attested. A commonly cited theory states that the phrase meant “money consisting of salt”, because, supposedly, Roman soldiers were sometimes paid in salt, but there is no evidence for either of these claims from ancient sources. Another is that the phrase meant “money used to buy salt [and other miscellaneous items]”.

Noun

A fixed amount of money paid to a worker, usually calculated on a monthly or annual basis, not hourly, as wages. Implies a degree of professionalism and/or autonomy.

Verb

To pay on the basis of a period of a week or longer, especially to convert from another form of compensation.

Adjective

Saline.

For The Public Domain Review the item's OWN page had to carry article-level CC BY or CC BY-SA evidence: the publisher states that some of its Articles are "published under more restrictive terms", so the site-wide statement was never used to decide an item, and any "All rights reserved", "Reprinted by permission" or NonCommercial-only item was excluded. For Wiktionary the CC BY-SA statement carried on each page was required, and third-party or non-free content (fair-use quotations, usage examples carrying quotations, File/Image links) was excluded from the stored body rather than assumed compatible. No image, audio or other media is reused from either source: imageReference is null for every item.
